queue.tree_name: The Tabunoki of the Goryo Shrine at Sakanoshita
queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the big evergreen behind the shrine at the Enoden level crossing, 20 metres tall, its new leaves coming out bronze in spring before they turn.
queue.story: The Enoden train runs across this shrine's approach. Goryo Shrine at Sakanoshita sits behind Hase, and the level crossing at its torii is one of the most photographed spots in Kamakura, because the little green and cream train passes within a couple of metres of the shrine steps. Most people are there for the train. The tabunoki behind it is 20 metres tall, a Kamakura City Natural Monument and one of the six Kamakura trees on Kanagawa's list of a hundred notable trees. queue.tree_name: The Centenary Horse Chestnut of Parque de Doña Casilda
queue.recognise: Not individually pinned within the park; look for a mature horse chestnut among the imported specimens, easiest to spot in May when it flowers white.
queue.story:
In a park stocked with trees from five continents, the specimen the guides keep naming is a horse chestnut. Parque de Doña Casilda de Iturrizar is Bilbao's largest central park, 115,200 square metres of ponds, pergola and imported botany begun in 1907, and its planting runs to dozens of species from all over the world. The one that gets singled out is Aesculus hippocastanum, a Balkan tree so common on northern European streets that children in four countries grow up throwing sticks at it, and here it is always described the same way: centenario, over a hundred years old.

queue.tree_name: The Monterey Cypress at Bishops Knoll
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the Victorian iron railings still standing round its trunk, which is over seven metres in girth. It stands inside Bishops Knoll Wood, among the old grounds of the demolished Knoll mansion.
queue.story:
The house whose garden this cypress grew up in has been gone for half a century, and its railings have not. Bishops Knoll Wood was once the grounds of The Knoll, a mansion built in the late 19th century for Peter Prankerd and demolished in the 1970s. The Monterey cypress still stands inside the Victorian ironwork that was put round it, a fence guarding a garden that no longer exists.

It has grown into what the Bristol Tree Forum calls a colossal specimen. The Forum measured the trunk at 7.1 metres round, and the Woodland Trust, which now owns the wood, gives it a girth of over seven metres.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the smooth grey stems reaching right over the path and the Bagheera panther fountain, with a cable in the crown. It stands on the Lagoon Path, the biggest beech in the Garden.
queue.story:
One of this beech's branches grew so long that it put down roots of its own in the flower bed beyond the path. The Friends of the Public Garden, who care for the Garden's trees alongside the city, described it in 2019 as a venerable specimen reaching out over the walkway and over the Bagheera fountain, with that rooted limb cabled back to its many-stemmed trunk to keep the whole thing together.

The Garden holds fourteen beeches, and the Friends say some of them date from its original plantings in the 1870s. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped two-lobed leaves on the biggest ginkgo in the Garden, about 4.3 metres round. It stands on the west side, about 10 metres from the bur oak and near the pagoda tree.
queue.story:
For most of the year this is a big tree in a garden full of big trees. For a day or two in November it is the one everybody stops for. Ginkgos turn butter gold all at once, then let go of nearly every leaf in a single drop, and a crown this size leaves a carpet of yellow fans across the lawn on the Garden's west side.

It is the largest ginkgo the city has recorded in the Public Garden and on Boston Common, 53.8 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, against 39.4 for the next one down. That figure comes from the city's tree inventory alone. No register or published account gives this tree's size or history, so treat the measurement as one good source rather than a settled fact.

queue.tree_name: The Wellingtonias by the Lower Pond, Combe Dingle
queue.recognise: You can recognise them as two very tall giant sequoias standing together, the thicker one, 7.1 metres round, on the stream side. They stand on the slope beside the stream near the lower pond in Combe Dingle.
queue.story:
Two Californian giants stand thirty metres apart at the bottom of a Bristol valley, beside a stream and a small pond. The thicker of the pair measures 7.1 metres round, which makes it, according to the Bristol Tree Forum, the largest of the three Wellingtonias on the Blaise Castle Estate. Its partner, about 30 metres away, is 6 metres round.

Wellingtonia is the British name for the giant sequoia, the species of the biggest trees on Earth in the Sierra Nevada, and in Britain it is a newcomer. The Forum's account is that seed reached the Veitch nursery in 1855. It dates the smaller of these two at about 150 years. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the big deeply lobed leaves and acorns in fringed cups, the broadest of the Garden's six bur oaks. It stands on the west side, about 10 metres from the big ginkgo.
queue.story:
Macrocarpa means big fruit, and this oak's acorns sit in cups edged with a shaggy fringe. It is the broadest of the Public Garden's six bur oaks, 53.1 inches across in the city's tree inventory, about 4.2 metres round. The next one down is 41.4.

That inventory is the only record of this tree's size. No register lists it and nothing published gives its history, so the figure stands on one good source. It is still a big oak by any standard for a city garden, and it has a lot of company. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its low, sprawling dome of branches running almost horizontally from the base, walked under rather than looked up at. It stands in the Jardim Engenheiro Luis da Fonseca.
queue.story: Two metres round the trunk, three and a half metres tall, and a crown eleven metres wide. Those numbers describe a tree that decided early on to spend its life going outwards rather than up, and the result in this waterfront garden is a low sprawling dome of long branches running almost horizontally from the base, which you walk under rather than look up at. The parish calls it a living monument, and it is the strangest thing on this page. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the broad spreading crown of fine compound leaves over a thick fissured trunk, almost five metres round. It stands on the Arlington Street side, about 45 metres from the dawn redwood.
queue.story:
Only one Japanese pagoda tree in Massachusetts is bigger than this one. The state's register measured it in January 2023 at 196 inches round, almost five metres, and 72 feet tall, and ranked it second of its kind in the Commonwealth. The city's own inventory of Public Garden trees agrees on the trunk, and has no other pagoda tree in the Garden anywhere near its size.

The tree does its best work late in the year. Pagoda trees flower in late summer, sending out sprays of cream blossom in August, when almost nothing else in bloom is a tree. On the Arlington Street side, this broad, spreading crown becomes one of the few things in flower overhead.

queue.recognise: A bare-looking conifer with a swollen, buttressed trunk at the University of Deusto's main entrance, facing the Guggenheim across the river.
queue.story:
A tree from the swamps of the American south stands at the front door of a Basque university, looking across the river at the Guggenheim. Bald cypress belongs in standing water in Louisiana and Florida, and this one has spent its life on a paved forecourt in rainy Bilbao, at the entrance to the 1886 main building of the Universidad de Deusto.

The Bilbao history site Absolut Bilbao puts it at nearly 25 metres tall, with a crown more than eight metres across and a trunk around three metres thick. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its four trunks standing in a ring inside a low wall. It stands in St Erfyl's churchyard in the centre of Llanerfyl.
queue.story:
What looks like four yews standing in a circle is reported to be a single tree. The trunks at St Erfyl's measure 10.67 metres around all four together, and DNA work is said to show they are one organism, even though three of the stems are recorded as female and one as male.

It has been admired for a long time. Lewis's Topographical Dictionary of Wales called it one of the finest yew-trees in the principality, and an account of 1872 named it the mother yew of Montgomeryshire. Its legend is older still. St Padarn is said to have left his staff, Cyrwen, here in the late sixth or early seventh century, and the yew grew from it.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, nearly 18 metres round, under a crown some 29 metres across. It stands at the end of the short Big Spruce trail from the Rain Forest Resort Village on South Shore Road.
queue.story:
This is the biggest Sitka spruce on record anywhere, and it is a few minutes' walk from a resort car park. American Forests lists it as the champion of its species, and by volume it ranks among the largest trees of any kind in the continental United States outside California's redwoods and sequoias.

The numbers are the kind that stop meaning anything until you stand next to them. Nearly 18 metres round the trunk. About 58 metres tall. A crown reaching some 29 metres across. Visitor sources usually give its age as around a thousand years, and that is a loose figure passed from one writer to the next rather than anything counted, so read it as somewhere between eight and twelve centuries. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk suspended over a gap in the bluff, held up by an arch of bare roots with a hollow beneath. It stands on the beach a few hundred feet to the right of the Kalaloch Campground access.
queue.story:
There is nothing under this tree. A creek has cut through the bluff beneath it and carried the soil away, and the Sitka spruce now hangs over the gap on an arch of its own exposed roots, with open air where the ground used to be. Locals call the hollow underneath the root cave.

It is one of the most photographed single trees on the Washington coast, and it has been a known sight for a long time. Staff at Kalaloch Lodge say people have been coming to look at it since at least the 1950s, and that it is probably much older than that. Nobody has dated it or measured it, so how old it really is stays an open question. If you know, tell us.

queue.recognise: You are looking for three yews, not the four Wordsworth counted. The largest is 7.5 metres round, more than the other two combined, and its crown is hollowed. The grove is fenced against sheep above Seathwaite.
queue.story:
William Wordsworth called them "those fraternal Four of Borrowdale, joined in one solemn and capacious grove," and for two centuries visitors have climbed the Cumbrian hillside above Seathwaite looking for exactly that number. They will find three. The fourth yew died at some point nobody recorded, its sex and its story lost with it.

The largest survivor, dated by dendrochronology to roughly 1,500 years old, measures about 7.5 metres round, more than the other two combined. queue.tree_name: The Bundle-planted Sessile Oak, Bishops Knoll
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the several fused stems that make one broad trunk, seven metres round. It stands close to the Bramble Lane entrance among apple and other fruit trees, partly screened by young ash.
queue.story:
This oak may be six trees pretending to be one. The Woodland Trust thinks it was planted as a bundle, six or so young oaks set in a single hole, which over the centuries fused into one trunk. That would explain why it is so portly, seven metres round. The Bristol Tree Forum agrees it may have been a bundle planting, noting that its several stems do not appear to grow from an old pollard cut, the other usual reason an oak ends up with many trunks.

queue.tree_name: The Grapevine of the Royal Hotel
queue.recognise: In the hotel's beer garden: one twisted grey trunk rising from a brick bed between the benches, its arms trained along steel pipes into a leaf roof over the whole courtyard.
queue.story:
In the courtyard of the Royal Hotel on Miller Street, Gilgandra, one grapevine roofs the whole beer garden. A reader who sent us its photograph wrote: "The Royal Hotel beer garden boasts the famous grape vine - believed to have been planted in the early 1900's as it was reported to be well established when the 1904 extensions were done. It still bares grapes each year and provides great cool, summer shade."

The hotel itself was built in 1892 as the Bridge Hotel, and it is a heritage-listed country pub. The reader puts the vine at about 130 years old and its trunk at 300 centimetres round; those are their figures, and we have found no other record of the vine yet.

queue.recognise: At the end of the trail at the edge of a meadow: a thick russet trunk behind a wooden rail, hung with grey dead lower limbs, its double-topped crown standing above every pine and fir around it.
queue.story:
Big Bear Lake's visitor bureau dates this lodgepole pine's germination to about 1560 and puts it at 452 years old, more than 110 feet tall and 22 feet round the trunk, with a bulbous base 36 feet in circumference. It is one of the largest lodgepole pines known in California, and it stands in a meadow in the San Bernardino Mountains south of Big Bear Lake, at the end of a short forest trail.

The reader's photograph stands at the foot of the trunk, which rises thick and russet-barked out of the undergrowth, hung all over with grey dead limbs that droop like curtains from the lower crown. queue.tree_name: The Blackbutt of Bird Tree Road
queue.recognise: A huge pale-barked eucalypt ringed by a timber boardwalk, its base flaring out like a buttressed column with a small dark hollow low on one side, the trunk rising straight and unbranched far into the rainforest canopy.
queue.story:
A reader sent this blackbutt with a GPS fix taken beside Bird Tree Road, inside Middle Brother National Park, west of Kendall on the New South Wales north coast, and gave it a girth of 11 metres and an age of about 300 years.

Those are the figures the New South Wales government gives for the Bird Tree, one of two blackbutts here it calls among the biggest in the state: 69 metres high and 11 metres round. The National Trust's tree register estimates the Bird Tree at about 300 years. The other giant on the same loop walk, Benaroon, is rated the largest blackbutt in Australia, with a girth of 15 metres.
